opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was the "Visualizing and Understanding Recurrent Networks" work I did with Andrej Karpathy and Fei-Fei back around 2015. What really grabbed us was that character-level LSTMs were producing surprisingly convincing output. You'd train one on the Linux kernel source, and it would generate C code that almost looked real. Brackets would mostly match, indentation looked reasonable, there were comments and function signatures. So the obvious question was: how is it doing that? What's actually going on inside?

Code turned out to be a great testbed, because it has a lot of explicit, long-range structure that you can check. If you open a bracket, you need to close it, possibly hundreds of characters later. You need to know whether you're inside a string or a comment. Indentation depends on how deeply nested you are. Those are concrete, measurable things, so you can go hunting for them in the hidden state.

The fun part was that when we looked at individual cells, some of them were really interpretable. There was a cell that turned on inside quotes and off outside them. There were cells that seemed to track line length so the model knew when to insert a newline. There were cells that tracked indentation depth or whether you were inside an if statement. Nobody told the model to learn those things. It just discovered them, because they were useful for predicting the next character.

That said, it was only a fraction of the cells. A lot of them looked like noise to a human, which was an early hint that representations are mostly distributed and you can't expect everything to line up neatly with concepts we have names for. We also did error analysis comparing the LSTM against n-gram baselines, to see which kinds of mistakes went away with the LSTM's longer memory, and it really was those long-range structural dependencies.

Looking back, it feels like an early version of what people now call mechanistic interpretability. The tools were much cruder and the models were tiny, but the basic instinct was the same: these models are doing something structured, and we should open them up and look instead of treating them as black boxes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that was the work I did with Andrej Karpathy and Fei-Fei Li back around 2015, the "Visualizing and Understanding Recurrent Networks" paper. And honestly the thing that drew me in was that at the time, recurrent nets were kind of a black box that everyone was excited about but nobody could really explain. Andrej had written that blog post, "The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks," where he trained character-level models on Shakespeare and Wikipedia and the Linux kernel source, and the samples were shockingly coherent. You'd look at generated C code and it would have balanced braces, properly closed comments, plausible-looking variable names. And the obvious question was: how? It's just a character-level model. It sees one byte at a time. Where is it keeping track of all that structure?

So we did what felt like the most direct thing, which was to just go look at the cells. Take the hidden state of the LSTM, pick a single cell, and color the input text by that cell's activation as it reads through. And what was compelling was that a handful of them were really interpretable. There was a cell that would turn on when you entered a quoted string and turn off when the quote closed. There was one that tracked the depth of nested parentheses or brackets. There was one that seemed to count position in a line, so it would ramp up as you got further from a newline, which makes sense if you need to predict when a line break is coming. In the code models you'd see cells that basically lit up inside comments, or inside if-statements.

And the reason code specifically was so nice as a testbed is that it has real long-range structure with a ground truth. If you open a brace, you have to close it. If you start a comment, you have to end it. So you could actually measure whether the model was getting those dependencies right and at what distance it started to fail. We did these error analyses where we compared against n-gram models, and you could see that the LSTM's advantage was concentrated in exactly those long-range cases, like closing a brace that was opened a hundred characters earlier. The n-gram just couldn't do it, and the LSTM mostly could.

I think the broader thing that I found satisfying was that it demystified the model a little bit without making it boring. Most of the cells were not interpretable, to be clear. The majority were kind of a mess, which is its own lesson. But the fact that some of them had landed on these clean, almost hand-designed-looking features, purely from next-character prediction, was a real glimpse of the idea that if you just push a model to predict text well enough, it ends up having to build internal machinery that tracks the structure of that text. That intuition has obviously scaled up in ways none of us anticipated, but the seed of it was right there in a few hundred LSTM cells reading Linux source code.

r001.rationale: The response describes an LSTM cell whose activation tracked the depth of nested parentheses while reading code, which communicates whether parentheses were open.

astra-6.text:
What I found compelling was that code gives you these really concrete things to look for. There are brackets that need to match, indentation, strings, comments—all this structure that the model has to keep track of if it’s going to predict the next character well.

So you could look inside the LSTM and ask, is it actually tracking any of that? And you could find individual cells whose behavior seemed to correspond to something interpretable, like whether you were inside a quoted string or how far you were indented. Nobody explicitly told the model to represent those things. It was just trained to predict text.

That was exciting because it gave us a way to connect the model’s internal state to something we understood about the task. It wasn’t a complete explanation of how the model worked, but it was a concrete foothold.

sol-6.1.text:
What was compelling was that you could train an LSTM on raw source code, just predicting the next character, and it would pick up structure that you hadn’t explicitly taught it. It would learn things like indentation, brackets, and when it was inside a string or a comment.

So the question was: how is it keeping track of that? When we looked inside, we could find individual cells whose activity seemed to correspond to some of those properties. That gave us a concrete connection between the model’s internal state and something we understood about the input. It was a way to start asking what the network had learned beyond just whether its output looked plausible.
